Two-thirds of the companies on the Forbes AI 50 list now use some form of usage-based pricing, reflecting AI’s variable costs and unpredictable demand. At the second annual Monetize conference last month, Metronome CEO and Cofounder Scott Woody put it more bluntly: today’s leading companies operate in ways that would seem “alien” to traditional SaaS businesses. These companies are iterating much faster on pricing, prioritizing market share over ARR, and pursuing multiple go-to-market strategies at once.

More than 300 leaders from fast-moving companies like Replit, Fin, Snowflake, and Clay came together at Monetize to trade notes on pricing, cost management, and scaling AI products as customer expectations change. Across sessions, five approaches for how companies are now approaching the economics of AI monetization came up repeatedly.

Hybrid pricing: Packaging usage with subscriptions and credits

A year ago, it was common to expect usage-based pricing to displace subscriptions. Businesses are still using them, just in a new way.We’re seeing more companies using subscriptions to package up variable usage, often through credits.

Aisling O’Reilly, Fin’s director of product for monetization, described the evolution of her own company’s pricing models. The company evolved from a platform subscription to a hybrid model, introducing outcome-based pricing when it launched Fin AI Agent. Initially, customers paid for each support conversation resolved by the agent. As the product expanded into actions like recommending products, qualifying leads, and booking meetings, its original (and only) billable metric became an insufficient representation of customer value. Fin introduced additional billable outcomes, letting customers choose the outcome they wanted from each conversation type and pay based on its value. Customers can commit to a pool of credits, then draw down against that pool across outcomes without having to forecast each one separately.

What’s emerging for Fin and many other companies is a layered model, with subscriptions for actions and predictability, usage-based pricing for agentic work, and credits to simplify multiple usage or outcome units.

Predictability is becoming a product feature

One of the biggest challenges with usage-based billing is giving customers more predictable costs. They need to understand what drives usage, anticipate spend, set spend limits, and connect usage to value. Many companies have addressed those requirements through in-product dashboards, predictions, and other types of tooling.

Snowflake Senior Director Ryan Campbell explained how he and his team help customers monitor and control their consumption through in-product tooling like forecasting, calculators, scenario builders, and usage visibility. Similarly, Stripe’s Head of Global Pricing and Commercialization, Sam Lee, described the usage control pane, where users can see alerts, set and adjust spending controls, and manage consumption, as a new standard.

Commercial terms can also offer more predictability while keeping charges tied to usage. Annual usage buckets, discounted overages, and first-year fixed contracts with follow-on true-ups all offer customers clearer controls to manage variable bills.

As bills become more unpredictable, strong usage controls become part of what customers are paying for. Those controls help build trust in both the company and the product.

Falling AI costs and rising usage call for flexible packaging

With advances in AI, companies are able to package the same product in different ways. Subscriptions can house lower-cost and rate-limited experiences, while usage-based billing can be used for more resource-intensive agent work. Replit uses both as model costs and agent workloads shift, said Michele Catasta, the company’s president and head of AI.

When Replit’s agents used to run for just a few minutes, the company charged 25¢ per agent checkpoint. But as runtimes grew, some jobs cost Replit several dollars while users still paid just 25¢. The company adopted usage-based billing to close the gap, aligning prices more closely with the amount of work performed by its agents.

This move solved one problem and introduced another: unpredictable spending and abrupt paywalls for users accustomed to a straightforward monthly subscription. As inference costs fell—due in part to increasingly capable open-source models and the pressure they put on frontier-model prices—Replit introduced a rate-limited Free Mode. This gives users the ability to keep building on a simple subscription. The company changes elements of its pricing several times a month, passing savings on to customers.

This opens up more flexible packaging beyond the one-product, one-pricing-model approach. Companies can combine subscriptions and usage-based billing, then adjust the mix as the underlying economics shift. That lets them offer versions of the same product at different speeds, prices, and service levels.

Finance’s new mandate: Proving AI value

While tokens might determine a company’s costs, it’s rare that they represent the value customers think they’re buying. In a session on how finance teams can measure AI’s value, Karan Parekh, Clay’s head of finance, said the company doesn’t want to be in the business of “upcharging and taxing tokens.” When pricing, Clay treats model tokens and third-party data as pass-through inputs, separate from the differentiated value its product provides.

Clay applies the same approach to evaluate its own internal AI investments. The sales team tracks productivity, the product team focuses on development time, and support teams measure throughput and customer satisfaction. Parekh’s team is comfortable with its own AI spending growing faster than revenue only if it’s producing something distinctive Clay couldn’t otherwise achieve.

Attribution is difficult when multiple tools and workflow changes contribute to the same result, making token-level ROI calculations misleading. Clay’s solution is to measure AI tooling against those function-specific targets, reviewing them quarterly to track whether those AI investments prove out. For finance teams, operational outcomes are a more useful lens than focusing on input costs.

Pricing information needs to be readable by both machines and humans

Agents are already influencing how products are discovered and evaluated, even if autonomous enterprise purchasing has yet to fully emerge.

To understand how buyers might encounter pricing in AI-generated answers, Kyle Poyar, founder of Growth Unhinged, tested how six AI engines presented pricing information for companies on the Cloud 100. He analyzed 7,600 AI-generated responses. For one unnamed company, negative pricing language appeared in 88% of responses. Without accessible pricing for this organization, LLMs resorted to scouring informal sources like Reddit and reported back prices ranging from $100–$2,400 per user, per month, a 24x difference.

Pricing information might be fully visible to humans who visit your site, but if it’s blocked from crawlers or rendered in a way agents can’t reliably interpret, it’s basically invisible. While autonomous enterprise procurement is still early, pricing now has two different audiences to serve. The person accountable for the purchase is still in the picture, but they’ve made room for the machine helping them evaluate the purchase.

AI monetization is becoming an adaptive system

AI products, model economics, and usage patterns are changing far too quickly for pricing to stay static. Across sessions, leaders described identifying what customers value, giving them more control over spending, and adjusting pricing and packaging as products and business economics change.

Watch the recorded sessions from Monetize 2026 for the full conversations with leaders from Replit, Fin, Snowflake, Clay, Growth Unhinged, and Stripe.

Token billing is useful infrastructure and, for almost every company, a bad customer-facing pricing model. In its simplest form, passthrough pricing charges customers for the model tokens their usage consumes, plus a markup on the underlying cost. If you’re building your pricing around that token consumption, you’re letting your costs determine your price.

That’s reflected in how our customers are using token billing today. They need it on the backend to track usage, manage markups, and protect their unit economics, but they don’t want those details defining how they price their product.

This gets at something I’ve been saying for a while: your invoice should be where you define your value to your customer.

Token-based billing has an invoice problem

This raises the obvious question: why did we build token billing in the first place? Because it’s a safeguard against runaway compute costs, and it’s easy to deploy and explain. For model providers, token usage is the product. For most other AI companies, token billing can be a useful place to start: tokens provide an obvious, countable basis for pricing. But neither subscription seats nor tokens accurately reflect the value your customer receives.

Token billing positions your product as a commodity markup on top of an actual commodity. It shows the customer an accounting of which models were used, how many tokens were consumed, and what markup was applied. But presenting your model mix, input costs, and margins to a customer misses the point. If their invoice shows that you used 10 models with a 10% markup on one, 5% on another, and 25% on another, you’ve defined your value as the difference between your price and somebody else’s model costs.

As those models become cheaper and more interchangeable, customers can challenge your markup or route around you entirely. Competition drives the markup, and potentially your business, toward zero.

A better model: Unified credits

Many of our customers are already using Metronome as a margin-tuning system, not just to deploy pricing models. They make model-routing decisions upstream, then send the resulting token usage to Metronome—either broken out by customer or attributed to a single aggregate customer for cost tracking. Our product then gives them visibility into token consumption so they can manage costs and tune their margins.

That gives companies control over their internal economics, but it doesn’t solve the invoice problem. They still need a presentation layer on top of the core modeling that translates the underlying usage into something tangible for customers. More companies are turning to a unified credit model.

A unified credit model creates a credit-based burndown. Customers draw down a common credit balance as they use different product operations, with each task consuming credits at its own rate based on the underlying token consumption. One operation might enrich a dataset, another might generate an image. In that case, the invoice can show the customer those enrichments or generated images, not the 10 models you used in the process and the markup applied to each.

The point isn’t to eliminate complexity; it’s to keep it behind the scenes. Metronome preserves token-level metering, so companies can continue routing models upstream and tuning for margin and performance as workloads change or new models are introduced. But with a unified credit model, your customer doesn’t have to parse all that complexity. On their invoice, the customer sees credits tied to the work the product performs, not tokens tied to the model costs.

Why output-based pricing is the ideal (and outcome-based pricing is a myth)

Unified credits are a stepping stone to output-based pricing, which is the best way to align AI consumption pricing with value today.

There are three common pricing metrics in AI. The first is an input, which is a cost, like a token.

The second is an outcome, which could mean the customer making more money, building more pipeline, or reducing churn. Outcomes can help you orient your product around customer value, but they’re difficult to turn into defensible pricing metrics.

Outcome-based pricing only works in a very limited set of circumstances and is largely a luxury reserved for the corporate super-rich. You either need monopoly-like power—enough control over the transaction and its underlying telemetry to measure the outcome, and enough market power to make customers accept that pricing—or a very high ticket price, since only very large contracts can justify the investment required to measure outcomes. At a high enough ticket price, you can afford to instrument a workflow end-to-end and prove mathematically that you’ve made it much more efficient: it requires fewer people, work gets done faster, or inventory turns more quickly. Every quarter, you can prove that value back to the customer and charge a fee as a function of that outcome.

For everyone else, outcome-based pricing is, for all intents and purposes, a myth. There’s a telemetry gap around what counts as the outcome, whether it occurred, and whether your product caused it.

Say, for example, I sell you a sales agent and charge you based on the revenue it generates. I’ve immediately invited a dispute over the relative value of human labor versus automated labor. Did the agent generate the sale or was it the sales rep? Was it marketing? Would the customer have purchased anyway? The outcome might be valuable, but it can’t be objectively attributed to the product.

The third way to price is on outputs.An output is an objective, verifiable metric, like generating an image or sending an email. Fin’s pricing, based on resolved support conversations, is considered the poster child for outcome-based pricing. I would argue it’s actually an output. The outcome of customer support is happy customers; a resolved support ticket is something you can objectively count.

All companies should do the same: define your output metric, call it an outcome, and convince the market that you’re right.

Where pricing is headed

Pricing models are slow to change because customers compare you with the rest of your competition. There’s a heavy penalty for departing from the herd.

But once a new model takes hold, the market can change very quickly. It’s Darwinian: a pricing model can look completely maladaptive, then suddenly become adaptive and spread through the category.

Three years ago, our team at Metronome predicted that hybrid pricing—some combination of seats plus usage—would become a prominent business model. We built support for it, and it went largely unused by our customers for around 18 months. Then, as of August 2026, roughly one in six (and growing) Stripe users that had crossed key revenue milestones were actively using or rolling out hybrid pricing. The model we’d been hypothesizing about for years seemed to catch on all at once.

Fin followed a similar pattern. Three years ago, almost no one in the AI customer-support category was talking about outcome-based pricing. Within a quarter of Fin introducing pricing based on resolved support conversations, all five of the leading companies in the category had committed to some version of outcome-based pricing.

Nothing changed, then everything changed. Once the product category and its buyers reached a certain level of maturity, the preference cascaded through the market.

As agents become more involved in both buying services and doing work, I suspect we’ll see the same thing with output-based pricing.

Subscription and seat-based pricing have been dominant thus far partly because they’re straightforward for humans to understand and compare. It’s easy to explain a fixed price per month or a fixed price per user to human buyers. An agent, on the other hand, can account for far more variables and match the price of each task more closely to its value.

One analogy for this trajectory is high-frequency trading. Trading algorithms operate at a level of speed and complexity that humans can’t. Something similar could happen with pricing. As agents increasingly evaluate and purchase services, pricing models won’t be limited by how much complexity a human buyer can handle. Agents also make the work itself easier to measure. Each task leaves an audit trail, which makes more activities observable and verifiable without a separate monitoring system.

As more work moves through agents, I expect the measurable outputs they produce to become pricing metrics—even if they’re still often marketed as outcomes.

El 20/10/2010 se celebró el primer Día Mundial de la Estadística, tal como se acordó por la Comisión de Estadística de Naciones Unidas en su 41° período de sesiones en febrero de 2010.

La Asamblea General de Naciones Unidas, en su resolución 69/282, decidió designar el día 20/10/2015 como el segundo Día Mundial de la Estadística, y estableció también celebrar el Día Mundial de la Estadística quinquenalmente en el día 20 de octubre. En esta resolución se reconoce la larga historia de las estadísticas oficiales, así como la importancia fundamental de que exista una infraestructura estadística nacional sostenible para producir indicadores fiables y oportunos del progreso de un país. Además, resalta la función decisiva que desempeña la información estadística oficial de alta calidad para el análisis y la adopción de decisiones normativas bien fundadas en apoyo del desarrollo sostenible.

¿Qué productos forman parte de la cesta del Índice de Precios de Consumo (IPC)? ¿Por qué algunos tienen más importancia que otros? ¿Y cómo refleja este indicador los cambios en nuestros hábitos de consumo?

En este segundo episodio de En Clave INE, Ignacio González Veiga, Subdirector General de Estadísticas Coyunturales del INE, explica cómo se configura y actualiza la cesta del IPC, qué productos y servicios incluye y cómo se recogen sus precios para medir su evolución.

El IPC es uno de los indicadores económicos más conocidos, pero su cesta va mucho más allá de los productos que compramos en el supermercado. Desde la alimentación, la ropa y la gasolina hasta los servicios bancarios, los restaurantes o las actividades de ocio, recoge una amplia variedad de bienes y servicios representativos del consumo de los hogares residentes en España.

A lo largo de la conversación, Ignacio González Veiga explica por qué la inflación no afecta de la misma manera a todos los hogares. Cada persona tiene sus propios hábitos de consumo y percibe las variaciones de precios de forma diferente. El episodio aborda también el concepto de ponderación, que determina la importancia de cada producto o grupo dentro del IPC en función del gasto que realizan los hogares.

La evolución de la cesta del IPC permite, además, observar cómo cambian nuestras costumbres. Productos como los aguacates, las plataformas de streaming o los servicios de reparto de comida a domicilio se han incorporado a medida que han ganado relevancia en el consumo, mientras que otros, como las máquinas de coser, los DVD o las corbatas, han dejado de ser representativos.

El episodio recorre también los distintos grupos de bienes y servicios que integran el IPC y aclara algunas dudas habituales, como por qué se incluyen las rebajas, los impuestos o los automóviles, pero no la compra de vivienda. Asimismo, explica cómo se tienen en cuenta los cambios de calidad de los productos para que las variaciones registradas reflejen la evolución real de sus precios.

Por último, se detalla cómo obtiene el INE la información necesaria para elaborar este indicador. A la recogida tradicional de precios en establecimientos se suman nuevas técnicas, como la extracción de datos de páginas web (web scraping) y el uso de información procedente de las ventas de los comercios (scanner data), que permiten ampliar y mejorar la información disponible para el cálculo del IPC.

Varios expertos del INE participaron a primeros del mes de septiembre en el XLII Congreso Nacional de Estadística, Investigación Operativa y Ciencia de Datos (SEIO 2026) celebrado en Santiago de Compostela.

Rocío Fuente, subdirectora general del Laboratorio de datos en el INE, presentó la ponencia "ES_DataLab: Laboratorio de datos para contribuir al desarrollo de la investigación", en la que se expusieron los principales objetivos, avances y retos de esta iniciativa.

ES_DataLab constituye la infraestructura de acceso seguro a datos para investigación impulsada por el INE con la colaboración de otros organismos públicos como la Secretaría de Estado de la Seguridad Social y Pensiones, el Banco de España, la Agencia Estatal de la Administración Tributaria o el Servicio Público de Empleo Estatal.

Su objetivo es facilitar que la comunidad investigadora pueda desarrollar proyectos de alto valor científico utilizando información detallada procedente de distintas fuentes estadísticas y administrativas, siempre bajo estrictas garantías de confidencialidad y protección de los datos.

La presentación puso de relieve el papel del INE como coordinador entre los organismos e instituciones que suministran información para fines de investigación, favoreciendo un modelo de colaboración que amplía las oportunidades de acceso a datos y potencia la generación de conocimiento basado en evidencias.

Fuente destacó el potencial crecimiento del catálogo de datos de ES_DataLab, lo que permitirá abordar investigaciones cada vez más relevantes para el análisis económico y social.

Imputación masiva

Miguel Ángel Martínez Vidal, Subdirector General de Formación, Análisis e Innovación en la Producción Estadística del INE fue uno de los moderadores de esta sesión, en la que también participaron Pedro García, Adrián Pérez y Javier de las Heras.

Javier de las Heras, director de programa de la Subdirección General de Estadísticas de Sectores Económicos del INE, presentó el trabajo desarrollado en su subdirección sobre la aplicación de técnicas de imputación masiva en las estadísticas estructurales de empresas.

Destacó las posibilidades que ofrece el uso de registros administrativos para reducir la dependencia de la información muestral, la valoración positiva de los primeros resultados y posibles soluciones para variables que no pueden obtenerse directamente de datos administrativos.

Muestreo y codificación

Pedro García Segador, consejero técnico de la Subdirección General de Metodología y Diseño de Muestras, expuso la presentación “Admisibilidad en muestreo con grafos de incidencia bipartitos”, en la que abordó el muestreo en poblaciones finitas modeladas como grafos, destacando cómo la incorporación de relaciones entre unidades resulta clave en metodologías no convencionales como el muestreo indirecto, en red o adaptativo.

Explicó cómo este marco permite tratar escenarios complejos con múltiples vías de observación y demostró formalmente la existencia de diversos estimadores admisibles alternativos al clásico estimador de Horvitz-Thompson.

Por su parte, Adrián Pérez Bote, jefe de área de la misma subdirección, realizó una presentación sobre marco metodológico para la construcción de codificadores de texto libre conforme a clasificaciones estadísticas oficiales.

En ella, hizo distintas aproximaciones convencionales a la codificación de textos según clasificaciones estadísticas, e introdujo métodos innovadores que vienen a complementar y adaptar las estrategias anteriores para adaptarlas a las necesidades de los institutos de estadística. También mostró la herramienta CodIA, y explicó qué metodología se había utilizado para su desarrollo.

Los líderes de las oficinas de estadística de los Estados miembros y Eurostat se reunieron los días 3 y 4 de septiembre en Dublín en una reunión de alto nivel, para debatir el diseño de un plan de simplificación del Sistema Estadístico Europeo (SEE).

Este plan tiene un doble objetivo: por un lado, reducir la carga de las estadísticas europeas a los informantes, especialmente las empresas, en línea con una agenda más amplia de simplificación regulatoria impulsada por las instituciones europeas para mejorar la eficiencia de las normas y reducir cargas administrativas a las empresas. Por otro lado, se persigue reducir la carga de trabajo y costes de producción que soportan las oficinas estadísticas, preservando la calidad, relevancia y fiabilidad de las estadísticas europeas.

La apertura del encuentro corrió a cargo de Jennifer Banim, directora general de la CSO de Irlanda. Seguidamente, Mariana Kotzeva, directora general de Eurostat, presentó las principales líneas de trabajo del futuro paquete de simplificación estadística preparado por la Comisión Europea.

A lo largo de la reunión se analizaron distintas oportunidades para reducir la carga asociada a la producción estadística. Algunos países reclamaron a Eurostat la necesidad de reducir requerimientos estadísticos, en términos de eliminación de variables, reducción de frecuencias o desagregaciones.

Más eficiencia y sostenibilidad

Elena Manzanera, presidenta del Instituto Nacional de Estadística, presentó la posición de España, basada en una estrategia de tres vías complementarias para avanzar hacia un sistema estadístico más eficiente y sostenible.

La propuesta, que fue bien recibida por los participantes, aboga por llevar a cabo un proceso de simplificación centrado en la racionalización del marco legislativo -con el objetivo de eliminar duplicidades, armonizar definiciones, simplificar calendarios y mejorar la coherencia del marco normativo, entre otras medidas-, así como en una apuesta por la modernización de los procesos e infraestructura estadística. Y, en tercer lugar, en la reducción de requisitos estadísticos establecidos en la legislación europea, siempre preservando la relevancia y la capacidad para responder a las necesidades de información de los usuarios.

Simplificación y modernización

Los asistentes también debatieron otras medidas relacionadas con la simplificación de los sistemas de calidad y metadatos, la racionalización y modernización de las transmisiones de datos, así como el potencial del intercambio de datos entre países para evitar duplicidades y mejorar la eficiencia.

Las conclusiones de la reunión servirán de base para los próximos trabajos de Eurostat y de los Estados miembros en materia de simplificación estadística. En el más corto plazo, contribuirán a la preparación del futuro paquete de simplificación de la legislación estadística europea, que se espera se pueda aprobar en el primer semestre de 2027.

A medio plazo, se plantean medidas más estratégicas como la simplificación desde el diseño en la preparación de la legislación estadística de la UE, reforzar el principio de solicitar los datos solo una vez o potenciar el intercambio de datos entre Estados miembros.

El Betis Deportivo perdió por 0-2 en la Ciudad Deportiva Luis del Sol ante un Recreativo de Huelva que confirmó su condición de líder. Los goles de José Carlos y Ale Marín prolongan la mala racha de los de Dani Fragoso, que encadenan cuatro jornadas sin ganar. El filial verdiblanco no pudo aprovechar la visita del Decano para asaltar la primera posición del Grupo IV de Segunda RFEF. El conjunto onubense se impuso por 0-2 y dejó patente su superioridad durante buena parte del encuentro.

El equipo blanquiazul tomó el control desde el comienzo. Su presión dificultó la salida de balón de los locales, que apenas encontraron espacios para progresar y tuvieron problemas para acercarse al área rival. En cambio, el Recreativo generó peligro con continuidad y pudo marcharse al descanso con una ventaja mayor. La actuación de Manu González evitó que el marcador se desequilibrara antes. El guardameta, que disputaba su segundo partido de la temporada, respondió con varias intervenciones de mérito, aunque no pudo impedir el tanto de José Carlos. El excentral verdiblanco adelantó a los visitantes pasada la media hora con un lanzamiento de falta raso que atravesó la barrera y sorprendió a la defensa bética.

El Betis Deportivo encontró algo más de presencia ofensiva en el tramo final del primer tiempo. Migue Romero evitó el segundo tanto del Recre al despejar un balón bajo palos y, poco después, Morante dispuso de una oportunidad para empatar tras un saque de esquina, pero no consiguió conectar el remate en buenas condiciones. La última acción destacada antes del descanso llegó con una reclamación de penalti por parte del conjunto local. Los verdiblancos pidieron la pena máxima por unas posibles manos de José Carlos dentro del área, en una acción en la que el defensor acudió al suelo para cortar un pase de Mario Navarro. El colegiado no señaló nada y el partido llegó al intermedio con ventaja visitante.

Ale Marín sentencia tras el descanso

Dani Fragoso introdujo cambios para intentar modificar el desarrollo del encuentro, pero el Recreativo encontró el segundo gol poco después de cumplirse la hora de partido. El Borussia Dortmund afrontará su duelo de Champions League ante el Real Betis después de superar una exigente prueba en la Bundesliga. El conjunto dirigido por Niko Kovac empató 2-2 en su visita al Bayern de Múnich, en una nueva edición del clásico alemán, y confirmó que atraviesa un buen momento de forma. Los amarillos fueron capaces de reaccionar en dos ocasiones y evitaron la derrota gracias a un gol de Fábio Silva en el tramo final. El resultado mantiene a ambos equipos igualados a 18 puntos después de ocho jornadas, aunque el Bayern conserva el liderato por su mejor diferencia de goles. El Dortmund, por tanto, llegará al compromiso europeo sin conocer todavía la derrota en el campeonato doméstico y con la confianza que supone haber competido de tú a tú ante el principale aspirante al título.

El Bayern llevó la iniciativa durante buena parte de la primera mitad y encontró el premio en el minuto 38. Konrad Laimer aprovechó una pérdida de Felix Nmecha en el centro del campo, combinó con Michael Olise y terminó superando a Gregor Kobel para establecer el 1-0. Antes, el Dortmund había celebrado un tanto de Jobe Bellingham, pero la intervención del VAR anuló la acción por fuera de juego y una falta previa sobre el guardameta Urbig. El equipo de Kovac tuvo que resistir el empuje local y también pudo encajar algún gol más antes del descanso.

La segunda parte comenzó con otra oportunidad para los muniqueses, pero Harry Kane desaprovechó un penalti y envió el balón al larguero. El fallo permitió al Borussia mantenerse en el partido y recuperar terreno. Serhou Guirassy igualó el marcador en el minuto 60 desde los once metros, aunque la reacción visitante tuvo una respuesta inmediata. Seis minutos después, Dayot Upamecano aprovechó una prolongación de cabeza de Kane para devolver la ventaja al Bayern.

Cuando el encuentro parecía encaminado hacia el triunfo local, Kovac recurrió a Fábio Silva en el minuto 76. El delantero portugués, que sonó para el Betis durante el pasado mercado de verano, apareció en el 89' para recoger un segundo balón tras un saque de esquina y conectar un disparo cruzado con la derecha. Su tanto estableció el definitivo 2-2 y permitió al Dortmund llevarse un punto de Múnich.

El Borussia afronta su undécima participación consecutiva en la máxima competición continental y cuenta con un historial reciente especialmente sólido en el Signal Iduna Park. En sus últimos 24 encuentros como local en la Champions, el equipo alemán solo ha perdido dos: ante el Barcelona, por 2-3, en diciembre de 2024, y frente al Inter, por 0-2, en enero de 2026. En la pasada edición terminó decimoséptimo en la fase liga, con tres victorias, dos empates y tres derrotas, y quedó eliminado en los play off ante el Atalanta.

Manuel Pellegrini se mostró satisfecho por el trabajo del equipo al término de la victoria de su equipo ante el Málaga (2-1). El Betis sigue muy arriba, con 23 sobre 33 puntos posibles, y a pesar que terminó mirando al reloj ante el colista, abre una veda de once puntos con los aspirantes Celta y, sobre todo, Villarreal. Cuestionado sobre la relajación del equipo en la recta final, el 'Ingeniero' lo tuvo claro: "Yo creo que hicimos un gran partido hasta el 2-1 de ellos. El marcador nos apretó, pero supimos defender bien. El primer tiempo me dejó muy conforme. En el segundo buscamos salir a buscar el tercero y, ya con el 2-1, el equipo se apretó un poco. Era importante no perder el resultado. Dicho eso, Álvaro no tuvo grandes tapadas. Me dejó conforme". Estas han sido sus declaraciones:

Satisfecho con el partido

"Hasta el 2-1, el equipo tuvo la iniciativa, llegadas, dominio, control... Después sí, ellos tuvieron el control, pero no llegadas. No fue un problema de relajo, hay otro equipo que juega. Un rato en el que no tuvimos el mismo control, pero supimos defender".

La recuperación de Antony

"Antony no comenzó jugando porque tuvo unos problemas a mitad de semana. De a poco debe ir recuperando su nivel. Ha tenido una serie de cosas físicas y no tengo ninguna duda de que lo vamos a recuperar y va a ser el mismo Antony de siempre".

Ruibal

"Aitor nos da mucho, tiene bastante gol y es una alternativa para la punta que tenemos con Cucho lesionado. Me alegré mucho por él".

Parrott

"Lo veo como siempre: intentando mejorar. Todos los jugadores tienen buenos y malos partidos. Lo fuimos alternado con Deossa porque jugó muchos minutos con la selección. No tengo ninguna duda que va a retomar su nivel. Es un jugador muy luchador y que nos aporta mucho".

Roca

"Marc está haciendo una gran temporada. No es su puesto pero lo está tomando con seriedad y profesionalismo. Hemos hablado mucho con él. Me alegro por él; es un gran profesional y nos da mucho".

¿Ceballos al cien por cien?

"Sí. Dani ha mejorado mucho en las últimas semanas. Vamos intentando hacer rotaciones, no es hacerlo por hacerlo, sino buscando alternativas para estar vivos en las tres competiciones".

¿Su mejor año?

"Yo creo que dentro del rendimiento de LaLiga, es uno muy alto. No sé si lo hemos logrado en otras temporadas, con la Champions de por medio este año. El equipo ha tenido la madurez de no pensar sólo en los miércoles. Las comparaciones con otras temporadas no es justa hacerlas ahora, pero vamos por el camino correcto".

Mucho camino aún que recorrer

"Yo creo que uno no puede pasarse ni siquiera por la mente que tiene ya la clasificación para Europa el próximo año. No hemos llegado ni al primer tercio. Estamos siempre intentando buscar lo más arriba posible, pero el peor error que podemos cometer es relajarnos. No estamos pensando en eso, sino en estar lo mejor posible en todas las competiciones que disputamos. Vamos a jugar en Champions contra un equipo difícil, pero iremos a buscar, como siempre, el partido. Hay 200 ejemplos de equipos que han hecho una buena primera vuelta y se han quedado en la segunda".

BANGKOK, October 12, 2026 - The World Bank Group today launched its Philanthropy Hub, a new platform to deepen collaboration with philanthropic organizations and other partners.

The Philanthropy Hub is part of a broader World Bank Group effort to make it easier to move from innovative ideas and pilot projects to scaled solutions, and from isolated efforts to collective action. As a single-entry point to the World Bank Group, the Hub will identify the best opportunities for philanthropic capital, solutions, and knowledge. It will also help shape the future of philanthropy for development through knowledge sharing, innovative partnerships, and aligning capital around shared priorities.

The launch comes at a time of rising development needs and constrained public resources. Philanthropic organizations are playing an increasingly active role, bringing not just grant funding but also investment capital, expertise, and the ability to convene partners. This support is already making a difference, with organizations contributing to the World Bank Group initiatives such as Mission 300, Health Works, and Water Forward, with tangible results on the ground.

"As development needs grow and resources come under pressure, partnership matters more than ever. Philanthropic organizations bring deep expertise and innovative solutions that align closely with our core missions and jobs agenda. The Philanthropy Hub will connect ideas, resources and partners to take those solutions to scale, and to deliver for people and communities around the world," Paschal Donohoe, Managing Director and Chief Knowledge Officer, World Bank Group.

The Philanthropy Hub was launched at the first World Bank Group Philanthropy Forumduring the World Bank Group-IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok. Co-convened with Asian Venture Philanthropy Network, the Institute of Philanthropy, the OECD's netFWD, and the Philanthropy Asia Alliance by Temasek Trust, the Forum brought together more than 200 leaders from philanthropic foundations and networks, family offices, development institutions, and partner organizations.

  • Through AVPN’s extensive regional network, foundations, social investors and private-sector partners can join forces to support World Bank Group initiatives.   • Temasek Trust’s experience in mobilizing philanthropic capital, convening partners, and advancing innovative financing approaches will help develop scalable partnership models, anchored in World Bank Group priority initiatives such as AgriConnect, Health Works, and Water Forward.

SEOUL, October 20, 2026— The World Bank Group today launched its first digital strategy, bringing together its public and private sector capabilities to help developing countries expand affordable digital access, improve services, and create jobs.

The strategy addresses four priorities: expanding connectivity; making devices and data more affordable; strengthening digital services and skills; and helping countries build the foundations to benefit from artificial intelligence.

“Digital technology can help countries create jobs and make scarce resources go further. Realizing that potential requires a comprehensive approach—from reliable connectivity and affordable devices to digital skills and useful services,” said World Bank Group President Ajay Banga. “Our first digital strategy brings these pieces together, helping countries build the foundations to benefit from today’s digital tools and the promise of small AI—AI for the people.”

The launch comes as developing countries face twin challenges: constrained resources and a growing need for jobs. Over the next 10 to 15 years, 1.2 billion young people will reach working age in developing countries, while their economies are projected to create about 420 million jobs.

Digital technology can support job creation across the World Bank Group’s five priority sectors: infrastructure and energy, agribusiness, health care, tourism, and value-added manufacturing. It can help businesses reach customers, improve productivity, and access finance, while reducing the cost of delivering public services.

Yet substantial barriers remain. Over 2 billion people were offline globally in 2025. Only 23 percent of people in low-income countries used the internet, compared with 94 percent in high-income countries. Many people live within network coverage but cannot afford a smartphone or data, lack digital skills, or have limited access to services relevant to their needs.

The strategy sets out four areas of action:

  • Expand reliable connectivity. The World Bank Group will help countries address gaps across the network, from international cables and national connections to the networks serving homes, businesses, schools, and clinics. Its approach includes supporting shared infrastructure, encouraging competition, and using public finance and guarantees to help attract private investment into underserved markets. Where electricity and connectivity are both missing, the strategy supports planning them together.
  • Make devices and data more affordable. The strategy supports efforts to lower the cost of entry-level smartphones and broadband services that increase the cost of staying connected. Partnerships with manufacturers, mobile operators, financial institutions, and refurbishment businesses can help lower prices and expand responsible options for paying over time.
  • Expand digital services and skills. The World Bank Group will support reliable systems for digital identification, payments, and secure information-sharing that make public and private services easier to access. It will also help countries strengthen digital literacy and training linked to employment, enabling more people and small businesses to use technology safely and productively.
  • Build readiness for AI. The strategy will help countries strengthen connectivity, access computing resources, develop usable local data, and build skills. It emphasizes practical applications of “small AI”—tools adapted to specific tasks and local conditions, such as helping farmers identify crop disease, supporting health workers, or helping businesses manage inventory.

Safeguards—from privacy to cybersecurity and fraud protection—run across all four priorities.

The strategy brings together the World Bank Group’s financing, policy advice, private investment, and guarantees around country priorities. It also provides a basis for working with governments, technology companies, development partners, and philanthropy to extend digital opportunities to more people and businesses. Its aim is to help countries turn digital access into higher productivity, better services, and more opportunities to earn a living.

Complementing the strategy’s AI readiness and adaptation priority, the World Bank Group also announced the AI Infrastructure and Readiness Initiative. This is a new effort to help governments in emerging markets access affordable compute capacity—and put small AI to productive use—through shared, pay-as-you-go GPU infrastructure (specialized computing power used to develop and run AI applications), offering a practical alternative to standalone national data centers. The initiative will have an initial focus on Africa and Latin America, with knowledge partners including Cassava Technologies and NVIDIA.

WASHINGTON, October 26, 2026—Global progress on reducing extreme poverty has come to a standstill, and the world is at risk of falling further behind unless more and better jobs are created, according to the World Bank Group’s new Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2026. Without stronger per capita growth, the number of people in extreme poverty is projected to be higher in 2030 than it is today.

In 2026, about 811 million people — one in ten globally — live on less than $3.00 per person per day, a rate that has essentially not changed since the pandemic. To bring extreme poverty down to 3% by 2050, per capita economic growth would need to average around 4% per year — twice the rate achieved over the last 25 years.

“In countries where poverty is the highest, slow growth has held back job creation and limited opportunities for millions of people,” said Pablo Saavedra, World Bank Group Vice President for Prosperity. “We need to accelerate growth and enable the creation of more and better jobs as a key pathway out of poverty.”

The report notes that extreme poverty remains concentrated: More than half of the world's extremely poor live in just nine economies, and by 2030 an estimated 87% are projected to live in Sub-Saharan Africa or in fragile and conflict-affected situations.

Nearly half the global population — 3.7 billion people — still lives on less than $8.30/day, a number that has remained stagnant since 1990. The World Bank uses international poverty lines to track deprivation across different income contexts. The $3.00/day line measures extreme poverty and is based on the poverty standards used in low-income countries; the $8.30/day poverty line is the standard for upper-middle-income countries.

Poverty reduction requires both more and better jobs. The report identifies two mutually reinforcing priorities:

  • Closing employment gaps: Raising employment rates in poor households to 75% among working-age adults — which could be attained by closing the gender gap in employment rates — would reduce global extreme poverty by roughly one-fifth.
  • Closing earning gaps: Poor workers are concentrated in low-return activities such as smallholder farming and have lower education levels. Raising their education to the average attained by people above the extreme poverty line would increase predicted earnings by around 40% and cut extreme poverty nearly in half. Moving them into wage work or out of agriculture would cut poverty by about one-fifth.

The priorities differ across countries, but the goal is the same: Help farmers and small businesses earn more, create opportunities for better jobs, and bring more women into the workforce. More and better jobs are not only a path out of poverty. They are the foundation for economic security and a growing middle class.

“Even under challenging circumstances, progress is possible for improving lives and moving more people out of poverty,” said Michael Kremer, World Bank Group Chief Economist and Senior Vice President for Development Economics. “This report provides the framework for understanding the challenges and identifying the primary approaches for reducing poverty.”

Good morning.

Let me begin by thanking the Prime Minister and the people of Thailand for your generous hospitality. Deputy Prime Minister, Governor—thank you for the care and hard work you and your teams have put into these Meetings. And to our Chair, thank you for your leadership. It is a pleasure to be here with all of you.

In the months before I joined the World Bank Group in June 2023, three truths emerged clearly from conversations with shareholders, clients, private sector leaders, philanthropies, and others.

The challenges were great. Resources were limited. And the World Bank Group needed to face the wind.

Three years later, the wind has not eased. Conflicts persist. Fiscal space is tighter. Debt burdens have risen. And cost of essentials—from energy to fertilizer—remains high.

Meanwhile, a demographic transformation is unfolding.

Over the next 10 to 15 years, 1.2 billion young people will arrive at a job market projected to offer only about 400 million jobs.

This generation will shape the next century. The choices we make today will help determine how.

Those are the twin challenges we have been working to address:

Making scarce resources go further… while helping countries create jobs at scale.

They must be addressed together.

Over the past three years, I have used these Annual Meetings to lay out the work we were undertaking, changes we were making, and the ambition behind them.

This year, I want to focus on our progress—and where it is taking us.

The future of development will depend on bringing public finance, private investment, philanthropy, and technology together around what each country needs.

The partnership—and mix—should evolve as countries do.

Where needs and risks are greatest, public and concessional finance will remain essential. As countries grow stronger, private investment and access to markets should play a larger role. And to be clear success arrives when we are no longer needed by a country.

We have seen that journey. Thirty-five countries have moved from IDA to IBRD. Twenty-three are now IDA donors themselves. That is exactly what we want, and our strategy is built around what makes that progress possible.

It began with changing the World Bank Group itself.

We cut project preparation from 19 months to nine. Replaced 153 scorecard measures with 22 focused on impact. Increased pay-for-results financing from about one-third to half. Brought our public and private sector teams together around country-led strategies. And reengineered our balance sheet—creating more than $100 billion in additional IBRD lending capacity over a decade.

We are also making it easier for MDBs to work together.

The number of projects on our digital co-financing platform has tripled in two years to about 250 projects, seeking $138 billion in financing. We are cutting duplication by relying on each other’s work with the Asian Development Bank, Inter-American Development Bank and EBRD—and expanding that model.

Taken together, these changes give us greater capacity.

Our jobs strategy gives it direction.

The Jobs Council drew on experience across countries and sectors to identify policies and programs that create more and better jobs. The strategy that emerged rests on three pillars.

First, physical and human infrastructure. Employers need electricity, water, transport, and digital connections. People need health, education, and skills. Last year, we committed $40 billion—nearly one-third of our financing—to these foundations.

Second, regulatory and policy certainty. Businesses of every size depend on strong institutions, good governance, and clear rules—from simpler permits to predictable land laws. Last year, 30 percent of our public sector financing supported policy and institutional reform.

Third, scale. Even with strong foundations and clear rules, some risks still hold investment back. The Private Sector Investment Lab helped us focus on those barriers—from currency risk to access to finance—and strengthen the tools to address them: guarantees, equity, and local currency financing.

That is how we bring more private capital into development.

The results are beginning to show.

In FY22—the year before our workplan began—we mobilized roughly $35 billion in private capital. Last year: $112 billion. A threefold increase.

Alongside our own financing, total financing exceeded $230 billion.

Gains are being felt across the spectrum. Mobilization nearly tripled in lower-middle-income countries, quadrupled in upper-middle-income countries, and more than doubled across Africa.

Our challenge is that in low-income countries, where attracting commercial capital remains hardest, mobilization held flat. The path to the poorest and most fragile economies runs through their small businesses—often growing where larger companies have yet to take root. Our new MSME strategy aims to reach where opportunity is hardest to come by.

Participation is broadening too.

Last year, we mobilized capital from investors in 110 countries. The United States, United Kingdom, and India led the way. But investors also came from Romania, Chile, Poland, and Brazil.

More countries are attracting investment. More are supplying it.

Across it all, nearly 55 percent of our financing and the private capital we mobilized went to infrastructure and energy, agribusiness, health, tourism, and value-added manufacturing—sectors that we are focused on to create jobs.

And total World Bank Group climate co-benefits reached $96 billion—$48 billion came from private capital. $96 billion. One institution. One year.

But financing is only the beginning.

The real value is bringing that capacity together around what each country is trying to achieve. That is why country strategies and compacts matter. Roadmaps built around a country’s ambitions, the results we are trying to achieve together, and the investments and reforms required to get there.

The roadmap is bespoke. The discipline is consistent.

We show up bringing public and private sector capabilities together from the start. We use IDA and our balance sheet where public and concessional resources are needed, align with philanthropic and operational partners, and mobilize private capital where markets can support it.

Technology amplifies that work.

“Big AI” requires computing power, energy, data, specialized skills, and capital that put frontier models beyond many developing countries’ immediate reach.

But practical, or “small,” AI can help a farmer improve yields, a teacher tailor instruction, a health worker make better-informed decisions, or an entrepreneur reach new customers. So we are helping countries build the electricity, connectivity, device access, and safeguards to put those tools to work.

Skills are part of the package—connecting education and training more closely to the jobs and industries countries are building.

So are small businesses. Our MSME strategy, launched earlier this week, is designed to make firms more visible, connected, enabled, and funded—using digital records to improve access to finance, link smaller businesses to larger buyers and markets, and simplify the rules that allow them to grow.

Critically important, in fragile and conflict-affected settings, where conditions do not yet support larger companies, small businesses play an outsized role in creating jobs and laying the foundations for stability.

Embedded across everything we do—building resilient infrastructure and stronger institutions so progress lasts.

That is what we refer to as smart development.

Our method is producing results.

Start with energy.

Through Mission 300, our ambition with the African Development Bank is to bring electricity to 300 million people in Africa by 2030.

So far, 59 million have gained access. And the pace has accelerated—from 12 million in FY24, to 18 million in FY25, to 29 million last year.

But access is only part of the challenge. Homes, mines, factories, farms, and growing cities need reliable, affordable baseload power.

Our approach is balanced by design—a full mix of renewables, hydro, gas where appropriate, nuclear where it makes sense, transmission, grids, and storage. That includes supporting nuclear retrofits with the IAEA—the first such work in 50 years.

On water, our ambition with partners is to improve water security for up to one billion people by 2030, with the World Bank Group committed to 400 million. Twenty country compacts give us a path to reach 150 million people with clean water. Twenty more compacts are on the horizon.

In agriculture, private, philanthropic, and operational partners are working to help 300 million smallholder farmers move from subsistence to surplus by 2030, with the World Bank Group committed to 200 million. We built a pipeline to support 82 million farmers in AgriConnect’s first full year and are doing the spade work for the next 118 million.

Through HealthWorks—supported by the Japanese government—our ambition is to reach 1.5 billion people with quality, affordable health services by 2030. Roughly 600 million have already been reached. The same model is showing up in newer areas.

In critical minerals, we plan to multiply our business five times in five years. This week, we launched our first country compacts with MDB partners—to build local industries and keep more jobs and value at home. We’ve identified 20 countries who we could partner with on this work.

In economic corridors, we launched 52 new projects last year—up from 20 three years earlier. With partners like the European Commission’s Global Gateway, Italy's Mattei Plan, and the United States' DFC, we are bringing infrastructure and investment together.

The infrastructure connects places. The opportunity grows along the way.

In Lobito, a route principally for minerals is increasingly carrying farmers’ crops to markets—and helping towns and cities grow.

Different sectors. Different countries. Different solutions.

Same objective: advance development and generate jobs.

The next phase is execution at scale.

That means meeting private-sector clients where they invest and make decisions.

We are expanding our presence in New York, Frankfurt, Milan, and Tokyo—to originate opportunities, solve problems faster, and build stronger pipelines.

But stronger pipelines are only part of the answer.

Development finance has always faced a basic constraint: a dollar can only be in one place at a time. Finance a power project, and that capital is fixed for decades—unavailable for the next water system, rail corridor, or clinic countries need.

Meanwhile, pension funds, insurers, and sovereign wealth funds manage enormous pools of long-term capital looking for long-term investments.

We are making the introduction.

Six multilateral development banks are creating common ways to assess, document, package, and transfer investments—so a project we help finance today can be held by another investor tomorrow, freeing our capital for the next one.

Repeated across institutions and markets, that begins to create something much bigger: an emerging-market development asset class. If we get this right, the size of our balance sheet no longer defines the scale of our ambition—and we will bend the curve of development forever.

Let me end where this institution began.

In 1944, with the world still at war, delegates from forty-four nations gathered in the mountains of New Hampshire.

They had every reason to turn inward. Instead, they made a wager: that rebuilding one nation could strengthen others, and recovery was a shared responsibility.

They did not build a monument to charity. They built a Bank and a Fund.

They understood something we must never forget: prosperity is not a prize one nation wins from another. It is a fire that warms every house within reach.

As countries’ needs changed, this institution changed with them—developing new ways to finance development and support private enterprise.

Building knowledge over decades of work.

Our people carry that inheritance forward. Their expertise turns lessons from one country into possibilities for another. Their commitment turns those possibilities into progress.

They are the strength of this institution—and the reason we can ask more of its future.

Today, the challenge arrives as arithmetic: a gap of roughly 800 million jobs. Behind that number is a young woman with a degree and no employer. A young man with a trade and no electricity. A generation asking: is there a place for me?

A job is not a statistic. A job is dignity.

It is the difference between a young person who can build a future; and a young person awaiting one. Leave that potential unrealized, and the consequences cross border.

Give it opportunity, and the benefits cross borders too. That is why development is an investment in our collective future.

This institution is rising to that challenge.

Not to recreate the development model of the last generation—but to build one equal to the expectations of the next. A model that evolves as countries do.

Public money where markets can't yet reach. Private capital where it can create jobs and scale. Philanthropy to take early risk and unlock new ideas. Technology to make every dollar go further.

And a World Bank Group that brings it together around what each country needs. That is the future of development we are working toward.

The jobs gap is a projection. It does not have to be our future.

We have begun to show what this model can deliver. Now we must give it the scale and pace the next generation demands.

That future is ours to build.
